newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU 1998 set-aside seen unchanged after low stocks.
newsitem.headline: EU 1998 set-aside seen unchanged after low stocks.

text.p: Lower than expected European Union public grain stocks have reinforced the case for leaving the set-aside rate at five percent for the 1998 harvest, EU grain industry sources said.

On Thursday, the European Commission said stocks had fallen to 1.72 million tonnes net at the end of the intervention season on May 31, from 2.60 million tonnes at the start of the season on July 1, 1996, and from a 1993 peak of 33 million.

"Stocks are very low and production will most likely be below last year's level despite a bigger planted area," said one source, adding that the current crop situation pointed to output of around 200 million tonnes, against a record 200.7 million tonnes in 1996/97.
Lower yields due to drought, especially in Spain and Portugal, are expected to outweigh a 2.2 percent increase in area to 37 million hectares, according to trade forecasts.
Farmers put the area slightly higher at 37.9 million ha.
Crop prospects, but not the set-aside rate, were discussed at a meeting of EU grain traders and producers on Friday, the source added.
Commission grain officials, describing set-aside as a tool for managing grain markets, told the meeting it was too early for a clear picture of what the rate should be next season.
Finnish farmers only planted their crops a couple of weeks ago, whereas the harvest had already started in southern Spain and Portugal.
Commission officials could not be reached for comment.
EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler has said that he will present a proposal later this month on the 1997/98 set-aside rate so that farm ministers could take a decision at their meeting on July 22.

On Monday, Fischler told a European Parliament agricultural conference that if set-aside was the only system used to control production, it could rise to 25 percent in order to curb surpluses after east European countries start to join the EU in 2002.
Another option would be to lower prices and make EU grain more competitive on world markets, he added.
France has called for cereals set-aside to be cut to zero next season so as to help keep exports flowing.
But other countries, notably Germany, would prefer to raise set-aside so as to help maintain high producer prices.
All countries, strongly supported by the EU farmers' lobby COPA, want to fix the set-aside rate before the summer break in August.
